claim: In adult dentate gyrus neurogenesis, the switch from excitation to inhibition of the GABAergic input onto maturing newborn cells is crucial for their proper functional integration.
source: By analyzing a theoretical model, we show that the switch from excitation to inhibition of the GABAergic input onto maturing newborn cells is crucial for their proper functional integration.
evidence: The claim is supported by the theoretical model analysis presented in the manuscript, which demonstrates the functional role of the GABA-switch through computational simulations and mathematical analysis.

claim: When the GABAergic input is excitatory, cooperativity drives the growth of synapses such that newborn cells become sensitive to stimuli similar to those that activate mature cells.
source: When the GABAergic input is excitatory, cooperativity drives the growth of synapses such that newborn cells become sensitive to stimuli similar to those that activate mature cells.
evidence: The manuscript presents model simulations showing that during the early phase of maturation with excitatory GABAergic input, newborn cells develop receptive fields similar to mature cells.

claim: When GABAergic input switches to inhibitory, competition pushes the configuration of synapses onto newborn cells toward stimuli that are different from previously stored ones.
source: When GABAergic input switches to inhibitory, competition pushes the configuration of synapses onto newborn cells toward stimuli that are different from previously stored ones.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates through model simulations that after the GABA-switch, newborn cells become selective for novel patterns through competitive dynamics.

claim: Maturing newborn cells can code for concepts that are novel, yet similar to familiar ones.
source: This enables the maturing newborn cells to code for concepts that are novel, yet similar to familiar ones.
evidence: The manuscript shows through simulations that newborn cells become selective for novel digit patterns that are similar to pretrained patterns.

claim: The theory explains why adult-born dentate granule cells promote separation of similar but not distinct patterns.
source: Our theory of newborn cell maturation explains both how adult-born dentate granule cells integrate into the preexisting network and why they promote separation of similar but not distinct patterns.
evidence: The manuscript provides analytical and simulation results showing that newborn cells become selective for similar novel patterns but not distinct patterns.

claim: In the adult mammalian brain, neurogenesis is restricted to a few brain areas, such as the olfactory bulb and the dentate gyrus.
source: In the adult mammalian brain, neurogenesis, the production of new neurons, is restricted to a few brain areas, such as the olfactory bulb and the dentate gyrus (Deng et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Deng et al., 2010.

claim: The dentate gyrus is a major entry point of input from cortex, primarily entorhinal cortex, to the hippocampus.
source: The dentate gyrus is a major entry point of input from cortex, primarily entorhinal cortex (EC), to the hippocampus (Amaral et al., 2007), which is believed to be a substrate of learning and memory (Jarrard, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Amaral et al., 2007 and Jarrard, 1993.

claim: The hippocampus is believed to be a substrate of learning and memory.
source: The dentate gyrus is a major entry point of input from cortex, primarily entorhinal cortex (EC), to the hippocampus (Amaral et al., 2007), which is believed to be a substrate of learning and memory (Jarrard, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jarrard, 1993.

claim: Adult-born cells in dentate gyrus mostly develop into dentate granule cells.
source: Adult-born cells in dentate gyrus mostly develop into dentate granule cells (DGCs), the main excitatory cells that project to area CA3 of hippocampus (Deng et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Deng et al., 2010.

claim: Dentate granule cells are the main excitatory cells that project to area CA3 of hippocampus.
source: Adult-born cells in dentate gyrus mostly develop into dentate granule cells (DGCs), the main excitatory cells that project to area CA3 of hippocampus (Deng et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Deng et al., 2010.

claim: The properties of rodent adult-born DGCs change as a function of their maturation stage, until they become indistinguishable from other mature DGCs at approximately 8 weeks.
source: The properties of rodent adult-born DGCs change as a function of their maturation stage, until they become indistinguishable from other mature DGCs at approximately 8 weeks (Deng et al., 2010; Johnston et al., 2016; Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Deng et al., 2010 and Johnston et al., 2016, and by Figure 1a showing the integration timeline.

claim: Many adult-born DGCs die before they fully mature.
source: Many of them die before they fully mature (Dayer et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dayer et al., 2003.

claim: The survival of adult-born DGCs is experience dependent and relies on NMDA receptor activation.
source: Their survival is experience dependent and relies on NMDA receptor activation (Tashiro et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tashiro et al., 2006.

claim: Newborn DGCs have enhanced excitability compared to mature DGCs.
source: Initially, newborn DGCs have enhanced excitability (Schmidt-Hieber et al., 2004; Li et al., 2017) and stronger synaptic plasticity than mature DGCs, reflected by a larger long-term potentiation (LTP) amplitude and a lower threshold for induction of LTP (Wang et al., 2000; Schmidt-Hieber et al., 2004; Ge et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schmidt-Hieber et al., 2004 and Li et al., 2017.

claim: Newborn DGCs have stronger synaptic plasticity than mature DGCs, reflected by a larger long-term potentiation amplitude and a lower threshold for induction of LTP.
source: Initially, newborn DGCs have enhanced excitability (Schmidt-Hieber et al., 2004; Li et al., 2017) and stronger synaptic plasticity than mature DGCs, reflected by a larger long-term potentiation (LTP) amplitude and a lower threshold for induction of LTP (Wang et al., 2000; Schmidt-Hieber et al., 2004; Ge et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2000, Schmidt-Hieber et al., 2004, and Ge et al., 2007.

claim: After 4 weeks of maturation, adult-born DGCs have only weak connections to interneurons.
source: Furthermore, after 4 weeks of maturation adult-born DGCs have only weak connections to interneurons, while at 7 weeks of age, their activity causes indirect inhibition of mature DGCs (Temprana et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Temprana et al., 2015.

claim: At 7 weeks of age, the activity of adult-born DGCs causes indirect inhibition of mature DGCs.
source: Furthermore, after 4 weeks of maturation adult-born DGCs have only weak connections to interneurons, while at 7 weeks of age, their activity causes indirect inhibition of mature DGCs (Temprana et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Temprana et al., 2015.

claim: Newborn DGCs receive no direct connections from mature DGCs.
source: Newborn DGCs receive no direct connections from mature DGCs (Deshpande et al., 2013; Alvarez et al., 2016) (yet see Vivar et al., 2012), but are indirectly activated via interneurons (Alvarez et al., 2016; Heigele et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Deshpande et al., 2013 and Alvarez et al., 2016, with a note about conflicting evidence from Vivar et al., 2012.

claim: Newborn DGCs are indirectly activated via interneurons.
source: Newborn DGCs receive no direct connections from mature DGCs (Deshpande et al., 2013; Alvarez et al., 2016) (yet see Vivar et al., 2012), but are indirectly activated via interneurons (Alvarez et al., 2016; Heigele et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Alvarez et al., 2016 and Heigele et al., 2016.

claim: At about 3 weeks after birth, the GABAergic input from interneurons to adult-born DGCs switches from excitatory in the early phase to inhibitory in the late phase of maturation.
source: At about 3 weeks after birth, the γ-aminobutyric acid (GABAergic) input from interneurons to adult-born DGCs switches from excitatory in the early phase to inhibitory in the late phase of maturation (Ge et al., 2006; Deng et al., 2010) ('GABA-switch', Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ge et al., 2006 and Deng et al., 2010, and by Figure 1a showing the GABA-switch timeline.

claim: The GABA-switch is caused by a change in the expression profile of chloride cotransporters.
source: Analogous to a similar transition during embryonic and early postnatal stages (Wang and Kriegstein, 2011), the GABA-switch is caused by a change in the expression profile of chloride cotransporters.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang and Kriegstein, 2011.

claim: GABAergic inputs are crucial for the integration of newborn DGCs into the preexisting circuit.
source: It has been shown that GABAergic inputs are crucial for the integration of newborn DGCs into the preexisting circuit (Ge et al., 2006; Chancey et al., 2013; Alvarez et al., 2016; Heigele et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ge et al., 2006, Chancey et al., 2013, Alvarez et al., 2016, and Heigele et al., 2016.

claim: PV is expressed in 15–21% of all dentate GABAergic cells.
source: Overall, it has been estimated that PV is expressed in 15–21% of all dentate GABAergic cells (Freund and Buzsáki, 1996) and in 20–25% of the GABAergic neurons in the granule cell layer (Houser, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Freund and Buzsáki, 1996.

claim: PV is expressed in 20–25% of the GABAergic neurons in the granule cell layer.
source: Overall, it has been estimated that PV is expressed in 15–21% of all dentate GABAergic cells (Freund and Buzsáki, 1996) and in 20–25% of the GABAergic neurons in the granule cell layer (Houser, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Houser, 2007.

claim: 55% of GABAergic hilar cells express somatostatin.
source: Amongst the GABAergic hilar cells, 55% express somatostatin (SST) (Houser, 2007) and somatostatin-positive interneurons (SST-INs) represent about 16% of the GABAergic neurons in the dentate gyrus as a whole (Freund and Buzsáki, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Houser, 2007.

claim: Somatostatin-positive interneurons represent about 16% of the GABAergic neurons in the dentate gyrus as a whole.
source: Amongst the GABAergic hilar cells, 55% express somatostatin (SST) (Houser, 2007) and somatostatin-positive interneurons (SST-INs) represent about 16% of the GABAergic neurons in the dentate gyrus as a whole (Freund and Buzsáki, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Freund and Buzsáki, 1996.

claim: HIPP axons generate lots of synaptic terminals and extend as far as 3.5 mm along the septotemporal axis of the dentate gyrus.
source: HIPP axons generate lots of synaptic terminals and extend as far as 3.5 mm along the septotemporal axis of the dentate gyrus (Amaral et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Amaral et al., 2007.

claim: PV-expressing interneurons and SST-INs both target adult-born DGCs early (after 2–3 weeks) in their maturation.
source: PV-expressing interneurons (PV-INs) and SST-INs both target adult-born DGCs early (after 2–3 weeks) in their maturation (Groisman et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Groisman et al., 2020.

claim: PV-INs provide both feedforward inhibition and feedback inhibition to the DGCs.
source: PV-INs provide both feedforward inhibition and feedback inhibition (also called lateral inhibition) to the DGCs (Groisman et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Groisman et al., 2020.

claim: SST-INs provide lateral, but not feedforward, inhibition onto DGCs.
source: In general, SST-INs provide lateral, but not feedforward, inhibition onto DGCs (Stefanelli et al., 2016; Groisman et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stefanelli et al., 2016 and Groisman et al., 2020, and by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Adult-born DGCs are preferentially reactivated by stimuli similar to the ones they experienced during their early phase of maturation, up to 3 weeks after cell birth.
source: Adult-born DGCs are preferentially reactivated by stimuli similar to the ones they experienced during their early phase of maturation, up to 3 weeks after cell birth (Tashiro et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tashiro et al., 2007.

claim: The amount of newly generated cells per month is 3–6% of the total DGCs population.
source: Even though the amount of newly generated cells per month is rather low (3–6% of the total DGCs population [van Praag et al., 1999; Cameron and McKay, 2001]), adult-born DGCs are critical for behavioral pattern separation (Clelland et al., 2009; Sahay et al., 2011a; Jessberger et al., 2009), in particular in tasks where similar stimuli or contexts have to be discriminated (Clelland et al., 2009; Sahay et al., 2011a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to van Praag et al., 1999 and Cameron and McKay, 2001.

claim: Adult-born DGCs are critical for behavioral pattern separation.
source: Even though the amount of newly generated cells per month is rather low (3–6% of the total DGCs population [van Praag et al., 1999; Cameron and McKay, 2001]), adult-born DGCs are critical for behavioral pattern separation (Clelland et al., 2009; Sahay et al., 2011a; Jessberger et al., 2009), in particular in tasks where similar stimuli or contexts have to be discriminated (Clelland et al., 2009; Sahay et al., 2011a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clelland et al., 2009, Sahay et al., 2011a, and Jessberger et al., 2009.

claim: Adult-born DGCs are particularly important in tasks where similar stimuli or contexts have to be discriminated.
source: Even though the amount of newly generated cells per month is rather low (3–6% of the total DGCs population [van Praag et al., 1999; Cameron and McKay, 2001]), adult-born DGCs are critical for behavioral pattern separation (Clelland et al., 2009; Sahay et al., 2011a; Jessberger et al., 2009), in particular in tasks where similar stimuli or contexts have to be discriminated (Clelland et al., 2009; Sahay et al., 2011a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clelland et al., 2009 and Sahay et al., 2011a.

claim: The model network contains 100 DGCs and 25 GABAergic interneurons.
source: We model a small patch of cells within dentate gyrus as a recurrent network of 100 DGCs and 25 GABAergic interneurons, omitting the Mossy cells for the sake of simplicity (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The modeled interneurons correspond to SST-INs from the HIPP category.
source: The modeled interneurons correspond to SST-INs from the HIPP category, as they are the providers of feedback inhibition to DGCs through dendritic projections (Stefanelli et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2017; Groisman et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stefanelli et al., 2016, Yuan et al., 2017, and Groisman et al., 2020, and by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the model, each DGC projects to, and receives input from, a given interneuron with probability 0.9.
source: Hence, in the recurrent network model, each model DGC projects to, and receives input from, a given interneuron with probability 0.9.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a model parameter.

claim: Each of the 100 model DGCs receives input from a set of 144 model EC cells.
source: Each of the 100 model DGCs receives input from a set of 144 model EC cells (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: In the rat, the number of DGCs has been estimated to be about 10^6, while the number of EC input cells is estimated to be about 2·10^5.
source: In the rat, the number of DGCs has been estimated to be about 106, while the number of EC input cells is estimated to be about 2 · 105 (Andersen et al., 2007), yielding an expansion factor from EC to dentate gyrus of about 5.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Andersen et al., 2007.

claim: The expansion factor from EC to dentate gyrus is about 5.
source: In the rat, the number of DGCs has been estimated to be about 106, while the number of EC input cells is estimated to be about 2 · 105 (Andersen et al., 2007), yielding an expansion factor from EC to dentate gyrus of about 5.
evidence: The claim is derived from the cited cell numbers through calculation.

claim: The plasticity rule includes LTD whenever the presynaptic neuron is active and the postsynaptic firing rate is positive but below the threshold θ.
source: the second term on the right-hand side of Equation (1) describes long-term depression (LTD) whenever the presynaptic neuron is active and the postsynaptic firing rate is positive but below the threshold θ
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the description of the plasticity rule.

claim: The combination of LTP and LTD in the plasticity rule is consistent with experimental data.
source: Such a combination of LTP and LTD is consistent with experimental data (Artola et al., 1990; Sjöström et al., 2001) as shown in earlier rate-based (Bienenstock et al., 1982) or spike-based (Pfister and Gerstner, 2006) plasticity models.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Artola et al., 1990, Sjöström et al., 2001, Bienenstock et al., 1982, and Pfister and Gerstner, 2006.

claim: The third term in the plasticity rule implements heterosynaptic plasticity.
source: The third term on the right-hand side of Equation (1) implements heterosynaptic plasticity (Chistiakova et al., 2014; Zenke and Gerstner, 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chistiakova et al., 2014 and Zenke and Gerstner, 2017.

claim: The heterosynaptic term has a 'homeostatic' function.
source: In this sense, the third term has a 'homeostatic' function (Zenke and Gerstner, 2017), yet acts on a time scale faster than experimentally observed homeostatic synaptic plasticity (Turrigiano et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zenke and Gerstner, 2017 and Turrigiano et al., 1998.

claim: After pretraining with patterns from digits 3 and 4, out of the 100 DGCs, some have developed spatial receptive fields that correspond to different writing styles of digit 3, others receptive fields that correspond to variants of digit 4.
source: After pretraining with patterns from digits 3 and 4 in a variety of writing styles, we examine the receptive field of each DGC. Each receptive field, consisting of the connections from all 144 EC neurons onto one DGC, is characterized by its spatial structure (i.e. the pattern of connection weights) and its total strength (i.e. the efficiency of the optimal stimulus to drive the cell). We observe that out of the 100 DGCs, some have developed spatial receptive fields that correspond to different writing styles of digit 3, others receptive fields that correspond to variants of digit 4 (Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 1e.

claim: At the end of pretraining, the classification performance for patterns of digits 3 and 4 from a distinct test set is 99.25%.
source: At the end of pretraining, the classification performance for patterns of digits 3 and 4 from a distinct test set not used during pretraining is high: 99.25% (classification performance on digit 3: 98.71%; digit 4: 99.80%)
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results.

claim: Heterosynaptic plasticity ensures that the total strength of the receptive field of each selective DGC converges to a stable value which is similar for selective DGCs.
source: A detailed mathematical analysis (Materials and methods) shows that heterosynaptic plasticity in Equation (1) ensures that the total strength of the receptive field of each selective DGC converges to a stable value which is similar for selective DGCs confirming the homeostatic function of heterosynaptic plasticity (Zenke and Gerstner, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical analysis presented in the Materials and methods section and a citation to Zenke and Gerstner, 2017.

claim: Synaptic weights are intrinsically bounded without the need to impose hard bounds on the weight dynamics.
source: As a consequence, synaptic weights are intrinsically bounded without the need to impose hard bounds on the weight dynamics.
evidence: The claim is derived from the mathematical analysis of the plasticity rule.

claim: The spatial structure of the receptive field represents the weighted average of all those input patterns for which that DGC is responsive.
source: Moreover, we find that the spatial structure of the receptive field represents the weighted average of all those input patterns for which that DGC is responsive.
evidence: The claim is derived from the mathematical analysis.

claim: DGCs that do not develop selectivity have weak synaptic connections and a very low total strength of the receptive field.
source: The mathematical analysis also shows that those DGCs that do not develop selectivity have weak synaptic connections and a very low total strength of the receptive field.
evidence: The claim is derived from the mathematical analysis.

claim: The replacement of unresponsive neurons reflects the fact that unresponsive units have weak synaptic connections and, experimentally, a lack of NMDA receptor activation has been shown to be deleterious for the survival of newborn DGCs.
source: The replacement of unresponsive neurons reflects the fact that unresponsive units have weak synaptic connections and, experimentally, a lack of NMDA receptor activation has been shown to be deleterious for the survival of newborn DGCs (Tashiro et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tashiro et al., 2006.

claim: At the end of the early phase of maturation, newborn DGCs show a receptive field corresponding to a mixture of several input patterns.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis we find that, at the end of the early phase of maturation, newborn DGCs show a receptive field corresponding to a mixture of several input patterns (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: At the end of the late phase of maturation, newborn DGCs are selective for patterns from the novel digit 5, with different writing styles.
source: Therefore, in the late phase of maturation, competition drives the synaptic weights of most newborn DGCs toward receptive fields corresponding to different subcategories of the ensemble of input patterns of the novel digit 5 (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2b.

claim: During maturation, the L2-norm of the feedforward weights onto newborn DGCs increases.
source: During maturation, the L2-norm of the feedforward weights onto newborn DGCs increases (Figure 2e) indicating an increase in total glutamatergic innervation, e.g., through an increase in the number and size of spines (Zhao et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2e and a citation to Zhao et al., 2006.

claim: The distribution of firing rates of newborn DGCs is shifted to lower values at the end of the late phase compared to the end of the early phase of maturation.
source: Nevertheless, the distribution of firing rates of newborn DGCs is shifted to lower values at the end of the late phase compared to the end of the early phase of maturation (Figure 2c,d), consistent with in vivo calcium imaging recordings showing that newborn DGCs are more active than mature DGCs (Danielson et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2c,d and a citation to Danielson et al., 2016.

claim: The selectivity of newborn DGCs develops during maturation from broad to narrow tuning.
source: This reflects the development of the selectivity of our model newborn DGCs from broad to narrow tuning, consistent with experimental observations (Marín-Burgin et al., 2012; Danielson et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results and citations to Marín-Burgin et al., 2012 and Danielson et al., 2016.

claim: At the end of the late phase of maturation of newborn DGCs, the overall classification performance is 94.56% for the three ensembles of digits.
source: At the end of the late phase of maturation of newborn DGCs, we obtain an overall classification performance of 94.56% for the three ensembles of digits (classification performance for digit 3: 90.50%; digit 4: 98.17%; digit 5: 95.18%).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results.

claim: When all three digit ensembles are directly simultaneously pretrained starting from random weights, the overall classification performance is 92.09%.
source: In this case, the overall classification performance is 92.09% (classification performance for digit 3: 86.83%; digit 4: 98.78%; digit 5: 90.70%).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results for control 1.

claim: In control 2, previously unresponsive DGCs do not become selective for the novel digit 5, no matter during how many epochs patterns are presented.
source: In this case, we find that the previously unresponsive DGCs do not become selective for the novel digit 5, no matter during how many epochs patterns are presented (we went up to 100 epochs) (Figure 3b, control 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In control 3, where all DGCs keep plastic feedforward weights, learning of the novel digit induces a change in selectivity of mature neurons.
source: We observe that in the case where all neurons are plastic, learning of the novel digit induces a change in selectivity of mature neurons. Several DGCs switch their selectivity to become sensitive to the novel digit (Figure 3c), while none of the previously unresponsive units becomes selective for presented patterns (compare with Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The separation of the representation of '5's from '3's and '4's is better at end of the late phase when compared to the end of the early phase of maturation.
source: Noteworthy the separation of the representation of '5's from '3's and '4's is better at end of the late phase (Figure 4b) when compared to the end of the early phase of maturation (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by the visualization of DGC activity projections shown in Figure 4a,b.

claim: A larger network with 700 DGCs yields similar results to the network with 100 DGCs.
source: Indeed, a larger network with 700 DGCs, thus mimicking the anatomically observed expansion factor of about 5 between EC and dentate gyrus (all other parameters unchanged), yields similar results (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results reported in Supplementary file 3.

claim: The timing of the introduction of the novel stimulus is important for proper learning.
source: Interestingly, the timing of the introduction of the novel stimulus is important. In our main neurogenesis model with 100 DGCs, we introduce the novel digit 5 at the beginning of the early phase of maturation, which consists of one epoch of MNIST training patterns (all patterns are presented once). If the novel digit is only introduced in the middle of the early phase (half epoch), it cannot be properly learned (classification performance for digit 5: 46.52%).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results showing different classification performance depending on timing of novel stimulus introduction.

claim: A novel stimulus has to be introduced early enough with respect to newborn DGC maturation to be well discriminated.
source: Therefore, our model predicts that a novel stimulus has to be introduced early enough with respect to newborn DGC maturation to be well discriminated and that the accuracy of discrimination is better the earlier it is introduced.
evidence: The claim is a prediction derived from the simulation results showing timing-dependent learning.

claim: With 35 newborn DGCs, plastic mature DGCs improve classification performance.
source: We find that with 35 newborn DGCs (corresponding to the experimentally reported fraction of about 5%), plastic mature DGCs (with a learning rate half of that of newborn cells) improve classification performance (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results reported in Supplementary file 4.

claim: If the novel cluster is similar to pretrained clusters, the weight vector onto the newborn DGC at the end of the early phase of maturation lies at the center of mass of all the patterns across the three clusters.
source: If the novel cluster is similar to the pretrained clusters, the weight vector onto the newborn DGC at the end of the early phase of maturation lies at the center of mass of all the patterns across the three clusters.
evidence: The claim is derived from the mathematical analysis of the simplified model.

claim: If the novel cluster is distinct, the weight vector onto the newborn DGC at the end of the early phase of maturation is located at the center of mass of the two pretrained clusters.
source: By contrast, if the novel cluster is distinct, the weight vector onto the newborn DGC at the end of the early phase of maturation is located at the center of mass of the two pretrained clusters (Figure 5h).
evidence: The claim is derived from the mathematical analysis and shown in Figure 5h.

claim: Adult dentate gyrus neurogenesis promotes discrimination of similar patterns because newborn DGCs can ultimately become selective for novel stimuli, which are similar to already learned stimuli.
source: In conclusion, our model suggests that adult dentate gyrus neurogenesis promotes discrimination of similar patterns because newborn DGCs can ultimately become selective for novel stimuli, which are similar to already learned stimuli.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion derived from the model results.

claim: Newborn DGCs fail to represent novel distinct stimuli because they are too distinct from other stimuli already represented by the network.
source: On the other hand, newborn DGCs fail to represent novel distinct stimuli, precisely because they are too distinct from other stimuli already represented by the network.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion derived from the model results.

claim: For any dimensionality of the input space, even as high as 97-dimensional, the neurogenesis model performs better than the random initialization model.
source: We observe that for any dimensionality of the input space, even as high as 97-dimensional, the neurogenesis model performs better (has a lower total reconstruction error) than the random initialization model (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results reported in Supplementary file 5.

claim: The two-phase neurogenesis model is advantageous because the feedforward weights onto newborn cells can start at arbitrarily small values.
source: In summary, the two-phase neurogenesis model is advantageous because the feedforward weights onto newborn cells can start at arbitrarily small values; their growth is, during the cooperative phase, guided to occur in a direction that is relevant for the task at hand; the final competitive phase eventually enables specialization onto novel inputs.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion derived from the model analysis and comparison with control models.

claim: Experimental studies suggest that the switch from excitation to inhibition of the GABAergic input onto adult-born DGCs is crucial for their integration into the preexisting circuit.
source: While experimental studies, such as manipulating the ratio of NKCC1 to KCC2, suggest that the switch from excitation to inhibition of the GABAergic input onto adult-born DGCs is crucial for their integration into the preexisting circuit (Ge et al., 2006; Alvarez et al., 2016) and that adult dentate gyrus neurogenesis promotes pattern separation (Clelland et al., 2009; Sahay et al., 2011a; Jessberger et al., 2009), the link between channel properties and behavior has remained puzzling (Sahay et al., 2011b; Aimone et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ge et al., 2006 and Alvarez et al., 2016.

claim: The GABA-switch enables newborn DGCs to become selective for novel stimuli, which are similar to familiar, already-stored, representations.
source: Our modeling work shows that the GABA-switch enables newborn DGCs to become selective for novel stimuli, which are similar to familiar, already-stored, representations, consistent with the experimentally observed function of pattern separation (Clelland et al., 2009; Sahay et al., 2011a; Jessberger et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by the model results and citations to Clelland et al., 2009, Sahay et al., 2011a, and Jessberger et al., 2009.

claim: Previous modeling studies used supervised algorithmic learning rules.
source: However, our work differs from them in four important aspects. First of all, we implement an unsupervised biologically plausible plasticity rule, while many studies used supervised algorithmic learning rules (Chambers et al., 2004; Becker, 2005; Chambers and Conroy, 2007; Weisz and Argibay, 2009; Finnegan and Becker, 2015; DeCostanzo et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous modeling studies.

claim: Previous models bypassed the integration step by initialization of the connectivity weights toward newborn DGCs to random, yet fully grown values.
source: Second, as we model the formerly neglected GABA-switch, the connection weights from EC to newborn DGCs are grown from small values through cooperativity in the early phase of maturation. This integration step was mostly bypassed in earlier models by initialization of the connectivity weights toward newborn DGCs to random, yet fully grown values (Crick and Miranker, 2006; Aimone et al., 2009; Weisz and Argibay, 2009; Finnegan and Becker, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: Previous modeling works applied algorithmic weight normalization or hard bounds on the weights at each iteration step.
source: Previous modeling works either applied algorithmic weight normalization or hard bounds on the weights at each iteration step (Crick and Miranker, 2006; Aimone et al., 2009; Weisz and Argibay, 2009; Temprana et al., 2015; Finnegan and Becker, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: Earlier computational models of adult dentate gyrus neurogenesis obtained pattern separation independently of the similarity between the stimuli.
source: Finally, although some earlier computational models of adult dentate gyrus neurogenesis could explain the pattern separation abilities of newborn cells, separation was obtained independently of the similarity between the stimuli. Contrarily to experimental data, no distinction was made between similar and distinct patterns (Chambers et al., 2004; Becker, 2005; Crick and Miranker, 2006; Wiskott et al., 2006; Chambers and Conroy, 2007; Aimone et al., 2009; Appleby and Wiskott, 2009; Weisz and Argibay, 2012; Temprana et al., 2015; Finnegan and Becker, 2015; DeCostanzo et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous modeling studies.

claim: The early phase of maturation corresponds to cooperative unsupervised learning.
source: From a computational perspective, the early phase of maturation, when GABAergic inputs onto newborn DGCs are excitatory, corresponds to cooperative unsupervised learning.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the model mechanism.

claim: At the end of the early phase of maturation, the receptive field of a newborn DGC represents the center of mass of all input patterns that led to its activation.
source: At the end of the early phase of maturation, the receptive field of a newborn DGC represents the center of mass of all input patterns that led to its (indirect) activation.
evidence: The claim is derived from the mathematical analysis of the model.

claim: In the late phase of maturation, lateral interactions change from cooperation to competition, causing a shift of the receptive fields of the newborn DGCs toward novel features.
source: In the late phase of maturation, GABAergic inputs onto newborn DGCs become inhibitory, so that lateral interactions change from cooperation to competition, causing a shift of the receptive fields of the newborn DGCs toward novel features (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is derived from the model analysis and shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The integration mechanism is in agreement with the experimental observation that newborn DGCs are broadly tuned early in maturation, yet highly selective at the end of maturation.
source: This integration mechanism is in agreement with the experimental observation that newborn DGCs are broadly tuned early in maturation, yet highly selective at the end of maturation (Marín-Burgin et al., 2012; Danielson et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Marín-Burgin et al., 2012 and Danielson et al., 2016.

claim: The switch of lateral GABAergic input to newborn DGCs from excitatory to inhibitory provides a biological solution to the 'problem of unresponsive units'.
source: In the context of theories of unsupervised learning, the switch of lateral GABAergic input to newborn DGCs from excitatory to inhibitory provides a biological solution to the 'problem of unresponsive units' (Hertz et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the model mechanism in the context of unsupervised learning theory, supported by a citation to Hertz et al., 1991.

claim: The early cooperative phase of maturation can be seen as a smart initialization of the synaptic weights onto newborn DGCs.
source: Hence, the early cooperative phase of maturation can be seen as a smart initialization of the synaptic weights onto newborn DGCs, close enough to novel patterns so as to become selective for them in the late competitive phase of maturation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the model mechanism.

claim: The model results are in line with the classic view that dentate gyrus is responsible for decorrelation of inputs.
source: Our results are in line with the classic view that dentate gyrus is responsible for decorrelation of inputs (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Marr, 1971; Rolls and Treves, 1998), a necessary step for differential storage of similar memories in CA3, and with the observation that dentate gyrus lesions impair discrimination of similar but not distinct stimuli (Gilbert et al., 2001; Hunsaker and Kesner, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Marr, 1969, Albus, 1971, Marr, 1971, Rolls and Treves, 1998, Gilbert et al., 2001, and Hunsaker and Kesner, 2008.

claim: Dentate gyrus lesions impair discrimination of similar but not distinct stimuli.
source: Our results are in line with the classic view that dentate gyrus is responsible for decorrelation of inputs (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Marr, 1971; Rolls and Treves, 1998), a necessary step for differential storage of similar memories in CA3, and with the observation that dentate gyrus lesions impair discrimination of similar but not distinct stimuli (Gilbert et al., 2001; Hunsaker and Kesner, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gilbert et al., 2001 and Hunsaker and Kesner, 2008.

claim: The model predicts that NKCC1-knockout mice would be impaired in discriminating similar contexts or objects.
source: Therefore, our model predicts that NKCC1-knockout mice would be impaired in discriminating similar contexts or objects because newborn cells stay silent due to lack of indirect activation.
evidence: The claim is a prediction derived from the model mechanism.

claim: If newborn cells in NKCC1-knockout mice are activated by light-induced or electrical stimulation, they would become selective to novel patterns and discrimination abilities would be restored.
source: If, however, in the same paradigm newborn cells are activated by light-induced or electrical stimulation, we predict that they become selective to novel patterns. Thus discrimination abilities would be restored and newborn DGCs are likely to survive.
evidence: The claim is a prediction derived from the model mechanism.

claim: An absence of early excitation using NKCC1-knockout mice has been shown to strongly affect synapse formation and dendritic development in vivo.
source: An absence of early excitation using NKCC1-knockout mice has been shown to strongly affect synapse formation and dendritic development in vivo (Ge et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ge et al., 2006.

claim: A reduction in inhibition in the dentate gyrus through decrease in KCC2 expression has been associated with epileptic activity.
source: Conversely, a reduction in inhibition in the dentate gyrus through decrease in KCC2 expression has been associated with epileptic activity (Pathak et al., 2007; Barmashenko et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pathak et al., 2007 and Barmashenko et al., 2011.

claim: The proper timing of the GABA-switch has been shown to be crucial for sensorimotor gating and cognition.
source: An analogous switch of the GABAergic input has been observed during development, and its proper timing has been shown to be crucial for sensorimotor gating and cognition (Wang and Kriegstein, 2011; Furukawa et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang and Kriegstein, 2011 and Furukawa et al., 2017.

claim: Several experimental results have suggested that the switch is sharp and occurs within a single day, both during development and adult dentate gyrus neurogenesis.
source: Several experimental results have suggested that the switch is indeed sharp and occurs within a single day, both during development (Khazipov et al., 2004; Tyzio et al., 2007; Leonzino et al., 2016) and adult dentate gyrus neurogenesis (Heigele et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Khazipov et al., 2004, Tyzio et al., 2007, Leonzino et al., 2016, and Heigele et al., 2016.

claim: In hippocampal cell cultures, expression of KCC2 is upregulated by GABAergic activity but not affected by glutamatergic activity.
source: Furthermore, in hippocampal cell cultures, expression of KCC2 is upregulated by GABAergic activity but not affected by glutamatergic activity (Ganguly et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ganguly et al., 2001.

claim: The theory suggests that newborn cells have a coding rather than a modulatory role during dentate gyrus pattern separation function.
source: To conclude, our theory for integration of adult-born DGCs suggests that newborn cells have a coding – rather than a modulatory – role during dentate gyrus pattern separation function.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion derived from the model results.
